_comment: Directional rulings: code under `from` combined into a work distributed under `into`. Each cites an authority (slug from sources.json) with a verbatim quote and URL. verdict ∈ compatible | conditional | incompatible | disputed. Verified against the cited pages on 2026-09-18; a second adversarial pass on 2026-09-19 fetched every cited URL, flagged 16 fabricated or mis-anchored quotes and one wrong verdict (CC-BY-4.0), and surfaced ~70 missing high-frequency pairs (see docs/verification.md) — both fixed here.

rulings.quote: This is a free software license, compatible with version 3 of the GNU GPL.
rulings.rationale: GPLv3 section 7 permits the additional patent-termination and indemnification terms that Apache-2.0 carries, so Apache-licensed code may be included in a GPLv3 work. The combined work is distributed under GPLv3.
rulings.conditions: Keep the Apache NOTICE file and license headers; the combination as a whole is GPLv3.

rulings.quote: This is a free software license, compatible with version 3 of the GNU GPL.
rulings.rationale: Same as GPL-3.0-only: the 'or later' option does not remove GPLv3, under which Apache-2.0 code is compatible.
rulings.conditions: Keep the Apache NOTICE file and license headers.

rulings.quote: Please note that this license is not compatible with GPL version 2, because it has some requirements that are not in that GPL version. These include certain patent termination and indemnification provisions.
rulings.rationale: GPLv2 has no mechanism to accept Apache-2.0's patent-termination and indemnification clauses, so a GPL-2.0-only work cannot include Apache-2.0 code. The ASF agrees: 'the FSF has never considered the Apache License to be compatible with GPL version 2'. Fix: license your project GPL-2.0-or-later or GPL-3.0, or find an MIT/BSD alternative.

dissent.claim: The ASF states the same conclusion from its side: Apache-2.0 software cannot be included in GPLv2 works.

rulings.quote: However, if code is released under GPL "version 2 or later," that is compatible with GPLv3 because GPLv3 is one of the options it permits.
rulings.rationale: A GPL-2.0-or-later work may choose to be distributed under GPLv3, and under GPLv3 Apache-2.0 code is compatible (FSF license list, #apache2). The combined work is then GPLv3, not GPLv2.
rulings.conditions: Distribute the combined work under GPLv3 (or later). You can no longer offer the combination under GPLv2 alone.

rulings.quote: GPLv3 software cannot be included in Apache projects. The licenses are incompatible in one direction only.
rulings.rationale: Copyleft flows one way: a work that includes GPLv3 code must itself be GPLv3. It cannot be distributed under Apache-2.0.
rulings.conditions: Either relicense the project to GPLv3, or keep the GPL program as a separate process (see the 'separate program' rulings).

rulings.quote: No. Some of the requirements in GPLv3, such as the requirement to provide Installation Information, do not exist in GPLv2. As a result, the licenses are not compatible: if you tried to combine code released under both these licenses, you would violate section 6 of GPLv2.
rulings.rationale: GPL-2.0-only code cannot be relicensed to v3 without the copyright holder, and v2-only and v3 terms conflict. Linux (GPL-2.0-only) is the classic example.
rulings.conditions: Only works if the dependency is 'GPL-2.0-or-later' rather than 'only'.

rulings.quote: No. Some of the requirements in GPLv3, such as the requirement to provide Installation Information, do not exist in GPLv2. As a result, the licenses are not compatible.
rulings.rationale: Symmetric to the v2→v3 case: a GPL-2.0-only work cannot absorb GPLv3 code.
Same license on both sides.

rulings.quote: However, if code is released under GPL "version 2 or later," that is compatible with GPLv3 because GPLv3 is one of the options it permits.
rulings.rationale: The 'or later' grant lets the GPLv3 project take the dependency under GPLv3.

rulings.quote: However, if code is released under GPL "version 2 or later," that is compatible with GPLv3 because GPLv3 is one of the options it permits.
rulings.rationale: 'Version 2 or later' includes version 2 itself, so the code may be used under GPLv2 in a GPL-2.0-only work.
Same license on both sides.

rulings.quote: This is a lax, permissive non-copyleft free software license, compatible with the GNU GPL.
rulings.rationale: The FSF lists the Expat (MIT) license as GPL-compatible without version qualification, so it works for GPLv2 and GPLv3 alike.
rulings.conditions: Keep the MIT copyright and permission notice.

rulings.quote: This is a lax, permissive non-copyleft free software license, compatible with the GNU GPL.
rulings.rationale: Same as GPLv2: MIT is compatible with every GPL version.
rulings.conditions: Keep the MIT copyright and permission notice.

rulings.quote: The following licenses may be included within Apache products: ... MIT/X11-style licenses
rulings.rationale: MIT is a Category A license for the ASF, and its only condition (keep the notice) is compatible with Apache-2.0's notice requirement.
rulings.conditions: Keep the MIT copyright and permission notice (typically in NOTICE or the bundled LICENSE).

rulings.quote: A short and simple permissive license with conditions only requiring preservation of copyright and license notices.
rulings.rationale: Same license; only the notice must be preserved.
rulings.conditions: Keep the notice.

rulings.quote: Licensed works, modifications, and larger works may be distributed under different terms and without source code.
rulings.rationale: MIT allows use in proprietary, closed-source products as long as the notice is preserved.
rulings.conditions: Keep the MIT copyright and permission notice in the distributed product.

rulings.quote: Licensed works, modifications, and larger works may be distributed under different terms and without source code.
rulings.rationale: MIT places no restriction on the license of a work that includes it, so it may be folded into an AGPLv3 project. The combination is distributed under AGPLv3.
rulings.conditions: Keep the MIT notice.

rulings.quote: Yes to both. Mozilla currently does this with BSD-licensed code.
rulings.rationale: The Mozilla FAQ answers 'yes' for combining MPL-licensed code with BSD- and Apache-licensed code in the same executable; MIT is the same permissive shape (notice-only, no copyleft) and is treated the same way in practice.
rulings.conditions: MIT files stay MIT; only files that already contain MPL code stay MPL.

rulings.quote: This is a lax, permissive non-copyleft free software license, compatible with the GNU GPL.
rulings.rationale: The 'Modified BSD' license (3-clause) dropped the advertising clause that made the original BSD incompatible.
rulings.conditions: Keep the notice; do not use contributors' names to endorse the product.

rulings.quote: This is a lax, permissive non-copyleft free software license, compatible with the GNU GPL.
rulings.rationale: Unqualified GPL compatibility covers GPLv2.
rulings.conditions: Keep the notice; no endorsement using contributors' names.

rulings.quote: BSD (without advertising clause)
rulings.rationale: BSD without the advertising clause is Category A for the ASF.
rulings.conditions: Keep the notice.

rulings.quote: A permissive license similar to the BSD 2-Clause License, but with a 3rd clause that prohibits others from using the name of the copyright holder or its contributors to promote derived products without written consent.
rulings.rationale: BSD-3-Clause's only conditions (notice, no endorsement) are satisfiable inside an MIT-licensed project; it is routinely mixed with MIT code across the npm ecosystem.
rulings.conditions: Keep the notice; do not use the contributors' names to endorse the product without permission.

rulings.quote: A permissive license similar to the BSD 2-Clause License, but with a 3rd clause that prohibits others from using the name of the copyright holder or its contributors to promote derived products without written consent.
rulings.rationale: Permits proprietary use; the notice-and-no-endorsement conditions travel with the shipped copy.
rulings.conditions: Reproduce the notice and disclaimer in the documentation or materials of a binary distribution; no endorsement using contributors' names.

rulings.quote: This is the original BSD license with the advertising clause and another clause removed. ... It is a lax, permissive non-copyleft free software license, compatible with the GNU GPL.
rulings.rationale: The FreeBSD / 2-clause BSD license is GPL-compatible.
rulings.conditions: Keep the notice.

rulings.quote: A permissive license that comes in two variants, the BSD 2-Clause and BSD 3-Clause. Both have very minute differences to the MIT license.
rulings.rationale: choosealicense describes BSD-2-Clause as functionally near-identical to MIT.
rulings.conditions: Keep the notice.

rulings.quote: A permissive license that comes in two variants, the BSD 2-Clause and BSD 3-Clause. Both have very minute differences to the MIT license.
rulings.rationale: Notice-only condition, compatible with proprietary distribution.
rulings.conditions: Reproduce the notice and disclaimer in the distributed product's documentation or materials.

rulings.quote: BSD (without advertising clause)
rulings.rationale: BSD-2-Clause is Category A for the ASF.
rulings.conditions: Keep the notice.

rulings.quote: This is a lax, permissive non-copyleft free software license with a serious flaw: the 'obnoxious BSD advertising clause'. The flaw is not fatal; that is, it does not render the software nonfree. But it does cause practical problems, including incompatibility with the GNU GPL.
rulings.rationale: The advertising clause adds a requirement the GPL does not allow, so 4-clause BSD code cannot go into a GPL work.
rulings.conditions: Ask the copyright holder to relicense under BSD-3-Clause (UC Berkeley did this for its own code in 1999).

rulings.quote: This license is sometimes also known as the OpenBSD License. It is a lax, permissive free software license, and compatible with the GNU GPL.
rulings.rationale: ISC is functionally equivalent to MIT/2-clause BSD.
rulings.conditions: Keep the notice.

rulings.quote: It is a lax, permissive free software license, and compatible with the GNU GPL.
rulings.rationale: Unqualified GPL compatibility covers GPLv2.
rulings.conditions: Keep the notice.

rulings.quote: ISC
rulings.rationale: ISC is listed under Category A (may be included in Apache products).
rulings.conditions: Keep the notice.

rulings.quote: A permissive license lets people do anything with your code with proper attribution and without warranty. The ISC license is functionally equivalent to the BSD 2-Clause and MIT licenses, removing some language that is no longer necessary.
rulings.rationale: choosealicense states ISC is functionally equivalent to MIT. It is the npm default license and the single most common license in the ecosystem alongside MIT.
rulings.conditions: Keep the notice.

rulings.quote: A permissive license lets people do anything with your code with proper attribution and without warranty. The ISC license is functionally equivalent to the BSD 2-Clause and MIT licenses, removing some language that is no longer necessary.
rulings.rationale: Notice-only condition; compatible with proprietary distribution.
rulings.conditions: Keep the notice in the shipped copy.

rulings.quote: A permissive license lets people do anything with your code with proper attribution and without warranty. The ISC license is functionally equivalent to the BSD 2-Clause and MIT licenses, removing some language that is no longer necessary.
rulings.rationale: No restriction on the license of the combined work.
rulings.conditions: Keep the notice.

rulings.quote: The Zero-clause BSD License can operate as a free software license compatible with the GNU GPL, but if the copyright notice or license notice is removed from the program, it is not possible to safely rely on the license and users might even face liability.
rulings.rationale: Zero-clause BSD has no notice requirement of its own, and the FSF lists it as GPL-compatible, with a caveat: keeping the notice anyway avoids the liability risk the FSF flags for a stripped copy.
rulings.conditions: Not required by the license, but the FSF recommends keeping the copyright/license notice to avoid the liability gap it describes.

rulings.quote: The BSD Zero Clause license goes further than the BSD 2-Clause license to allow you unlimited freedom with the software without requirements to include the copyright notice, license text, or disclaimer in either source or binary forms.
rulings.rationale: No conditions at all; freely includable in an MIT project (this is how `tslib` reaches most TypeScript trees).
rulings.conditions: None.

rulings.quote: The BSD Zero Clause license goes further than the BSD 2-Clause license to allow you unlimited freedom with the software without requirements to include the copyright notice, license text, or disclaimer in either source or binary forms.
rulings.rationale: No conditions; safe in proprietary products.
rulings.conditions: None.

rulings.quote: 0BSD
rulings.rationale: Category A for the ASF.
rulings.conditions: None.

rulings.quote: Both public domain works and the lax license provided by the Unlicense are compatible with the GNU GPL.
rulings.rationale: Public-domain dedication with a permissive fallback.

rulings.quote: A license with no conditions whatsoever which dedicates works to the public domain. Unlicensed works, modifications, and larger works may be distributed under different terms and without source code.
rulings.rationale: No conditions; `tweetnacl` and other Unlicense packages appear in most MIT trees without issue.

rulings.quote: A license with no conditions whatsoever which dedicates works to the public domain. Unlicensed works, modifications, and larger works may be distributed under different terms and without source code.
rulings.rationale: No conditions; freely usable in proprietary products.

rulings.quote: Unlicense
rulings.rationale: Category A for the ASF.

rulings.quote: A license with no conditions whatsoever which dedicates works to the public domain.
rulings.rationale: No restriction on the license of the combined work.

rulings.quote: CC0 also provides a lax, permissive license as a fallback. Both public domain works and the lax license provided by CC0 are compatible with the GNU GPL.
rulings.rationale: The FSF recommends CC0 for public-domain dedications of software.

dissent.claim: CC0 is not OSI-approved: Creative Commons withdrew it from OSI review over its explicit patent-rights exclusion (clause 4(a)).

rulings.quote: The Creative Commons CC0 Public Domain Dedication waives copyright interest in a work you've created and dedicates it to the world-wide public domain. Use CC0 to opt out of copyright entirely and ensure your work has the widest reach.
rulings.rationale: Public-domain dedication; no license notice to preserve.

rulings.quote: The Creative Commons CC0 Public Domain Dedication waives copyright interest in a work you've created and dedicates it to the world-wide public domain.
rulings.rationale: No conditions; note it grants no patent rights (clause 4(a)), unlike a permissive license with an express patent grant.

rulings.quote: CC0
rulings.rationale: Category A for the ASF.

rulings.quote: Use CC0 to opt out of copyright entirely and ensure your work has the widest reach.
rulings.rationale: No restriction on the license of the combined work.

rulings.quote: This is a lax permissive non-copyleft free software license, compatible with the GNU GPL.
rulings.rationale: No conditions at all.

dissent.claim: WTFPL does not appear on the OSI's list of approved licenses.

rulings.quote: This is a free software license, and compatible with the GPL.
rulings.rationale: Zlib/libpng license is permissive and GPL-compatible.
rulings.conditions: Altered source versions must be plainly marked as such.

rulings.quote: A short permissive license, compatible with GPL. Requires altered source versions to be documented as such.
rulings.rationale: Only condition is marking altered source; freely includable in an MIT project (`pako` ships MIT AND Zlib code this way).
rulings.conditions: Document altered source versions as such.

rulings.quote: A short permissive license, compatible with GPL. Requires altered source versions to be documented as such.
rulings.rationale: Permissive; safe in proprietary products.
rulings.conditions: Document altered source versions as such.

rulings.quote: This is a lax, permissive non-copyleft free software license, compatible with the GNU GPL.
rulings.rationale: Boost's notice requirement applies to source only, not binaries.
rulings.conditions: Keep the notice in source distributions.

rulings.quote: This is a free software license and is compatible with the GNU GPL.
rulings.rationale: The Python 2.0.1+ license is GPL-compatible (versions 1.6b1 through 2.0 were not). npm packages usually declare this as PSF-2.0.

rulings.quote: Python Software Foundation License
rulings.rationale: Category A for the ASF; permissive with a notice requirement, includable in an MIT project (`argparse`, a transitive dependency of `js-yaml`, declares this).
rulings.conditions: Keep the PSF copyright and license notice; briefly summarise changes to the software if you modify and redistribute it.

rulings.quote: Python Software Foundation License
rulings.rationale: Permissive; usable in proprietary products.
rulings.conditions: Keep the PSF copyright and license notice.

rulings.quote: Permission to use, copy, modify, and distribute this software and its documentation for any purpose, without fee, and without a written agreement is hereby granted, provided that the above copyright notice and this paragraph and the following two paragraphs appear in all copies.
rulings.rationale: Structurally identical to the Expat/MIT permission grant (permissive, notice-only, no added restriction) — the same pattern the FSF calls GPL-compatible for the Expat and BSD-2-Clause licenses on its license list. The GNU license list does not name the PostgreSQL license specifically.

rulings.quote: This license is a free software license, compatible with the GPL thanks to the relicensing option in section 4(c)(ii).
rulings.rationale: Artistic 2.0 (Perl 6+) fixed the vagueness of Artistic 1.0.

dissent.claim: Artistic License 1.0 is NOT accepted by the FSF as a free software license ('too vague'), although the OSI approves it.

rulings.quote: We cannot say that this is a free software license because it is too vague; some passages are too clever for their own good, and their meaning is not clear.
rulings.rationale: The FSF does not consider Artistic 1.0 free or GPL-compatible; the OSI approved it in 1999 and still lists it. Perl itself avoids the problem by dual-licensing Artistic OR GPL.
rulings.conditions: Treat as incompatible unless the package is dual-licensed (e.g. 'Artistic-1.0-Perl OR GPL-1.0-or-later').

dissent.claim: The OSI lists the Artistic License 1.0 as an approved open source license.

rulings.quote: Yes, by creating a "Larger Work" under the terms of Section 3.3. In particular, three requirements must be met: The software must not be "Incompatible With Secondary Licenses." The Larger Work must be a combination of Covered Software with a work governed by one or more Secondary Licenses. You must "additionally distribute" under (L)GPL.
rulings.rationale: MPL 2.0 section 3.3 (the Secondary License mechanism, defined in section 1.12 as GPL 2.0+, LGPL 2.1+, or AGPL 3.0+) lets MPL-covered files be additionally distributed under a GPL-family license when combined into a Larger Work with GPL/LGPL/AGPL code.
rulings.conditions: The MPL files must not carry the 'Incompatible With Secondary Licenses' notice (Exhibit B); you must additionally distribute the MPL-licensed source under (L)GPL to your recipients.

dissent.claim: The FSF agrees: Mozilla Public License (MPL) version 2.0 is compatible with the GNU GPL, version 2, provided you use the built-in secondary-license mechanism.

rulings.quote: Mozilla Public License 2.0 (MPL 2.0)
rulings.rationale: The ASF puts MPL-2.0 in Category B: it may be included in binary form, but the MPL-covered files remain under MPL and modifications to those files must be released under MPL.
rulings.conditions: Keep the MPL files under MPL (file-level copyleft); disclose changes to those files; the rest of the project can stay Apache-2.0.

rulings.quote: May I combine MPL-licensed code and BSD-licensed code in the same executable program? What about Apache? Yes to both. Mozilla currently does this with BSD-licensed code.
rulings.rationale: MPL 2.0 is a 'file-level' copyleft license: the FAQ's own description says it 'requires that MPL-covered files remain under MPL, but allows those files to be combined with files under other licenses into a Larger Work.' The FAQ names BSD and Apache explicitly and answers 'yes to both'; MIT is the same permissive shape.
rulings.conditions: Modified MPL files must be released under MPL; keep MPL notices; your MIT files are unaffected.

rulings.quote: May I combine MPL-licensed code and proprietary code in the same program? Yes. MPL 2.0 permits MPL-licensed code to be combined with proprietary code in a Larger Work.
rulings.rationale: The MPL files must stay open (source available to recipients), the proprietary files need not.
rulings.conditions: Make the source of the MPL-covered files (including your modifications) available to recipients; keep notices.

rulings.quote: The Larger Work must be a combination of Covered Software with a work governed by one or more Secondary Licenses. You must "additionally distribute" under (L)GPL.
rulings.rationale: MPL 2.0 section 1.12 names 'GNU Affero General Public License, Version 3.0' as a Secondary License, so the same section 3.3 mechanism that covers GPL/LGPL also covers AGPL 3.0+.
rulings.conditions: The MPL files must not carry the 'Incompatible With Secondary Licenses' notice; additionally distribute the MPL source under AGPL.

rulings.quote: This is a free software license which is not a strong copyleft; unlike the X11 license, it has some complex restrictions that make it incompatible with the GNU GPL.
rulings.rationale: MPL 1.1 lacks the Secondary License clause that MPL 2.0 added. Only works if the code is explicitly dual-licensed (the old MPL/GPL/LGPL tri-license).
rulings.conditions: Check for a dual-license grant (section 13 of MPL 1.1).

rulings.quote: The EPL 2.0 allows the initial contributor to designate a 'Secondary License' (GNU GPL v2.0 or later) ... only if the Secondary License is specifically designated in Exhibit A.
rulings.rationale: Without an explicit GPL secondary-license designation in the EPL headers, EPL-2.0 is GPL-incompatible. The FSF: 'this license ... is not compatible with the GPL unless the secondary license is designated'.
rulings.conditions: The EPL files must include the Exhibit A secondary-license notice naming the GPL; then they may be used under GPL-2.0-or-later.

dissent.claim: The FSF lists EPL-2.0 as GPL-incompatible by default: it 'is not compatible with the GNU GPL ... unless the developer uses the Secondary License option'.

rulings.quote: The Eclipse Public License is similar to the Common Public License, and our comments on the CPL apply equally to the EPL.
rulings.rationale: The FSF's EPL 1.0 entry redirects to its Common Public License 1.0 entry, which says: 'This is a free software license. Unfortunately, its weak copyleft and choice of law clause make it incompatible with the GNU GPL.' EPL 1.0 has no secondary-license mechanism (that was added in EPL 2.0).

dissent.claim: This is a free software license. Unfortunately, its weak copyleft and choice of law clause make it incompatible with the GNU GPL.

rulings.quote: Eclipse Public License 2.0 (EPL 2.0)
rulings.rationale: Category B at the ASF: include in binary form only; modifications to EPL code go back under EPL.
rulings.conditions: Do not modify EPL sources without releasing those changes under EPL; keep notices.

rulings.quote: This is a free software license. It has a copyleft with a scope that's similar to the one in the Mozilla Public License, which makes it incompatible with the GNU GPL. This means a module covered by the GPL and a module covered by the CDDL cannot legally be linked together.
rulings.rationale: The ZFS-on-Linux problem: CDDL and GPL modules cannot be combined into one work.
rulings.conditions: Keep the CDDL component as a separately distributed module.

rulings.quote: If you statically link against an LGPLed library, you must also provide your application in an object (not necessarily source) format, so that a user has the opportunity to modify the library and relink the application.
rulings.rationale: LGPL lets a non-copyleft or proprietary application link to the library. Modifications to the library itself must be released under LGPL.
rulings.conditions: Link dynamically (or provide relinkable object code if static); release modifications to the LGPL library under LGPL; provide the LGPL library's source and license notice.

rulings.quote: If you statically link against an LGPLed library, you must also provide your application in an object (not necessarily source) format, so that a user has the opportunity to modify the library and relink the application.
rulings.rationale: Proprietary programs may use LGPL libraries under section 6 of LGPL 2.1 provided users can replace the library.
rulings.conditions: Dynamic linking (or relinkable object files); ship the library source + LGPL text; allow reverse engineering for debugging the modified library.

rulings.quote: If you statically link against an LGPLed library, you must also provide your application in an object (not necessarily source) format, so that a user has the opportunity to modify the library and relink the application.
rulings.rationale: Same linking rule as LGPL-2.1-only; 'or later' only widens which LGPL version applies.
rulings.conditions: Dynamic linking or relinkable object code; ship LGPL text and library source; give prominent notice of LGPL use.

rulings.quote: If you statically link against an LGPLed library, you must also provide your application in an object (not necessarily source) format, so that a user has the opportunity to modify the library and relink the application.
rulings.rationale: Proprietary use is allowed under the same linking rule.
rulings.conditions: Dynamic linking or relinkable object code; ship LGPL text and library source; give prominent notice of LGPL use.

rulings.quote: This is a free software license, but not a strong copyleft license... It is compatible with GPLv2 and GPLv3.
rulings.rationale: LGPL 2.1 section 3 lets any recipient convert the library to GPL (2 or later), so it fits inside a GPLv3 work.

rulings.quote: LGPLv3 is also incompatible with GPLv2
rulings.rationale: LGPLv3 is GPLv3 plus extra permissions; GPLv2-only cannot absorb GPLv3 terms.

rulings.quote: This is the latest version of the LGPL... It is compatible with GPLv3.
rulings.rationale: LGPLv3 is defined as GPLv3 with additional permissions, so removing them yields GPLv3.

rulings.quote: If you statically link against an LGPLed library, you must also provide your application in an object (not necessarily source) format, so that a user has the opportunity to modify the library and relink the application.
rulings.rationale: Same as LGPL 2.1 for linking; LGPLv3 section 4 spells out the 'Combined Works' terms.
rulings.conditions: Dynamic linking or relinkable objects; prominent notice that the library is used and is under LGPLv3; ship LGPL text and library source; permit modification of the library for the user's own use.

rulings.quote: If you statically link against an LGPLed library, you must also provide your application in an object (not necessarily source) format, so that a user has the opportunity to modify the library and relink the application.
rulings.rationale: Proprietary linking is allowed under the LGPLv3 Combined Works terms (section 4).
rulings.conditions: Dynamic linking or relinkable object code; ship LGPL text and library source; permit relinking.

rulings.quote: If you statically link against an LGPLed library, you must also provide your application in an object (not necessarily source) format, so that a user has the opportunity to modify the library and relink the application.
rulings.rationale: Same linking rule as LGPL-3.0-only. This is the common real case: sharp's bundled libvips binaries declare LGPL-3.0-or-later.
rulings.conditions: Dynamic linking or relinkable objects; prominent LGPL-use notice; ship LGPL text and library source.

rulings.quote: If you statically link against an LGPLed library, you must also provide your application in an object (not necessarily source) format, so that a user has the opportunity to modify the library and relink the application.
rulings.rationale: Proprietary apps may link an LGPL-3.0-or-later library under the same Combined Works terms.
rulings.conditions: Dynamic linking or relinkable object code; ship LGPL text and library source; permit relinking.

rulings.quote: It is compatible with GPLv2 and GPLv3.
rulings.rationale: LGPL-2.1 converts to GPL (2 or later); GPLv3-family compatibility extends to AGPLv3 per the FSF compatibility matrix note that 'each place the matrix states GPLv3, the same statement is true for AGPLv3 as well'.

rulings.quote: This is the latest version of the LGPL... It is compatible with GPLv3.
rulings.rationale: LGPLv3 converts to GPLv3; GPLv3 compatibility extends to AGPLv3 per the FSF's compatibility-matrix note.

rulings.quote: If a library is released under the GPL (not the LGPL), does that mean that any software which uses it has to be under the GPL or a GPL-compatible license? Yes, because the program actually links to the library. As such, the terms of the GPL apply to the entire combination.
rulings.rationale: Linking to a GPL library makes the whole combination GPL; an MIT-licensed distribution of that combination is not possible.
rulings.conditions: Relicense the project to GPL-3.0, or interact with the GPL program only as a separate process over a well-defined interface (see next ruling).

rulings.quote: If the two programs remain well separated, like the compiler and the kernel, or like an editor and a shell, then you can treat them as two separate programs... By contrast, pipes, sockets and command-line arguments are communication mechanisms normally used between two separate programs.
rulings.rationale: Running a GPL tool as a separate process (CLI, pipes, sockets) does not make your program a derivative work, per the FSF's own guidance. Bundling both in one distribution is 'mere aggregation'.
rulings.conditions: No linking, no shared address space, communication only via pipes/sockets/CLI args, and no 'intimate' data-structure sharing.

rulings.quote: Yes, because the program actually links to the library. As such, the terms of the GPL apply to the entire combination.
rulings.rationale: The single most consequential verdict a proprietary project can receive: linking (or otherwise combining) GPL-3.0-only code makes the whole combination GPLv3, which a closed-source product cannot satisfy.
rulings.conditions: Obtain a commercial/dual license from the copyright holder, replace the dependency, or interact with it only as a separate process (see the 'separate' ruling).

rulings.quote: If the two programs remain well separated, like the compiler and the kernel, or like an editor and a shell, then you can treat them as two separate programs... By contrast, pipes, sockets and command-line arguments are communication mechanisms normally used between two separate programs.
rulings.rationale: A proprietary product may shell out to a GPLv3 CLI tool as a genuinely separate process without becoming GPL itself.
rulings.conditions: No linking or shared address space; communicate only via pipes/sockets/CLI args/subprocess; do not statically or dynamically link the GPL binary.

rulings.quote: Yes, because the program actually links to the library. As such, the terms of the GPL apply to the entire combination.
rulings.rationale: Same rule as GPLv3: linking a GPL-2.0-only library forces the whole combination to be GPL-2.0.
rulings.conditions: Relicense the project to GPL-2.0(-or-later), or treat the GPL program as a separate process.

rulings.quote: If the two programs remain well separated, like the compiler and the kernel, or like an editor and a shell, then you can treat them as two separate programs.
rulings.rationale: Same mere-aggregation exception applies regardless of GPL version.
rulings.conditions: No linking; communicate only via pipes/sockets/CLI args.

rulings.quote: Yes, because the program actually links to the library. As such, the terms of the GPL apply to the entire combination.
rulings.rationale: A closed-source product cannot satisfy GPL-2.0's requirement that the whole combination be GPL.
rulings.conditions: Obtain a separate commercial license, replace the dependency, or use it only as a separate process.

rulings.quote: Yes, because the program actually links to the library. As such, the terms of the GPL apply to the entire combination.
rulings.rationale: 'Or later' only widens which GPL version the combined work may use; it never permits a non-GPL combination. The dependency's `license.gplCompatibility` field says 'compatible' (meaning: compatible with GPLv2 and GPLv3 projects) — do not read that as compatible with a non-GPL project.
rulings.conditions: Relicense the project GPL-2.0-or-later (or GPL-3.0), or use only as a separate process.

rulings.rationale: Same as above: 'or later' does not create a path into a proprietary combination.
rulings.conditions: Obtain a commercial license, replace the dependency, or use only as a separate process.

rulings.quote: Yes, because the program actually links to the library. As such, the terms of the GPL apply to the entire combination.
rulings.rationale: Same linking rule regardless of the 'or later' grant.
rulings.conditions: Relicense to GPL-3.0(-or-later), or use only as a separate process.

rulings.quote: Yes, because the program actually links to the library. As such, the terms of the GPL apply to the entire combination.
rulings.rationale: AGPL is GPLv3 plus a network-use clause; linking an AGPL library makes the combination AGPL (per the FSF's compatibility-matrix note that GPLv3 statements hold for AGPLv3 too), so it cannot be distributed under MIT.
rulings.conditions: Relicense to AGPL-3.0, or use the AGPL component as a separate service.

rulings.quote: If the two programs remain well separated, like the compiler and the kernel, or like an editor and a shell, then you can treat them as two separate programs.
rulings.rationale: Talking to an AGPL server/database as a genuinely separate process (its own network service) does not make your client program AGPL. If you modify the AGPL program itself and let users interact with the modified version over a network, section 13 requires you to offer its source.
rulings.conditions: No linking or shared process; if you modify and network-deploy the AGPL program itself, offer its Corresponding Source under AGPL section 13.

rulings.quote: GPLv3 software cannot be included in Apache projects.
rulings.rationale: The ASF's GPL policy (Category X) covers the whole GPL family including AGPL: any GPL-family code forces the combination to that license, which an Apache-2.0 project cannot be.
rulings.conditions: Separate process only, or relicense.

rulings.quote: Each of these licenses explicitly permits linking with code under the other license. You can always link GPLv3-covered modules with AGPLv3-covered modules, and vice versa. That is true regardless of whether some of the modules are libraries.
rulings.rationale: GPLv3 and AGPLv3 explicitly permit linking with each other. GPLv3 section 13 states that the GPL terms continue to apply to the GPL part, while AGPL section 13's network-source requirement applies 'to the combination as such' — so the combination carries the AGPL network obligation even though the GPL files stay GPL.
rulings.conditions: The combined work must satisfy AGPL section 13 (offer source to network users) for the combination as a whole.

rulings.quote: Each of these licenses explicitly permits linking with code under the other license. You can always link GPLv3-covered modules with AGPLv3-covered modules, and vice versa.
rulings.rationale: A GPL-3.0-only dependency may be included in an AGPLv3 project; the GPL files stay GPLv3, the combination as a whole carries the AGPL section 13 network obligation.
rulings.conditions: The AGPL section 13 network-source obligation applies to the combination even though the GPLv3 files themselves remain GPLv3.

rulings.quote: LGPLv3 is also incompatible with GPLv2
rulings.rationale: AGPLv3 is GPLv3 plus section 13; GPL-2.0-only cannot be combined with any GPLv3-family license, by the same v2/v3 incompatibility that blocks LGPLv3.
rulings.conditions: Only works if the dependency is GPL-2.0-or-later, which can move to the GPLv3 family.

rulings.quote: This is a free software license, compatible with version 3 of the GNU GPL.
rulings.rationale: AGPLv3 is GPLv3 plus section 13; Apache-2.0's compatibility with GPLv3 (FSF #apache2) extends to AGPLv3 per the compatibility-matrix note that GPLv3 statements hold for AGPLv3 as well.
rulings.conditions: Keep the Apache NOTICE file and headers; the combination as a whole is AGPLv3.

rulings.quote: Apache 2 software can therefore be included in GPLv3 projects, because the GPLv3 license accepts our software into GPLv3 works. However, GPLv3 software cannot be included in Apache projects.
rulings.rationale: Any GPL version inside an Apache-2.0 work forces the whole work to GPL; the ASF categorises all GPL variants as Category X (excluded).
rulings.conditions: Separate process only, or relicense.

rulings.quote: This is the license of the original JSON implementation ... It adds a clause mandating: 'The Software shall be used for Good, not Evil.' This is a restriction on usage and thus conflicts with freedom 0. The restriction might be unenforceable, but we cannot presume that. Thus, the license is nonfree.
rulings.rationale: The 'Good, not Evil' clause is a use restriction; the FSF calls the license nonfree and it is not OSI-approved.
rulings.conditions: IBM famously obtained a written exception to use JSON-licensed code for evil. Otherwise replace the package.

rulings.quote: This is a restriction on usage and thus conflicts with freedom 0.
rulings.rationale: You cannot pass on MIT permissions you were not granted; the 'Good, not Evil' restriction travels with the code.

rulings.quote: This is a non-copyleft free license that is good for art and entertainment works, and educational works. It is compatible with all versions of the GNU GPL; however, like all CC licenses, it should not be used on software.
rulings.rationale: The FSF states CC BY 4.0 is compatible with every GPL version, but advises against using any Creative Commons license on software — reserve it for the non-code assets (docs, art, data) shipped alongside code, and keep the attribution requirement.
rulings.conditions: Give appropriate credit, a link to the license, and indicate changes (CC BY 4.0 §3(a)); do not rely on this license for the code itself.

rulings.quote: It is compatible with all versions of the GNU GPL; however, like all CC licenses, it should not be used on software.
rulings.rationale: `caniuse-lite` (used by browserslist/autoprefixer/babel/postcss in almost every JS build) declares CC-BY-4.0 for its data. It may be bundled with proprietary software; only the attribution condition applies.
rulings.conditions: Give appropriate credit, a link to the license, and indicate changes.

rulings.quote: CC-BY (properly labeled)
rulings.rationale: CC-BY is Category B for the ASF: includable, but it must be clearly labelled as under a different license than the rest of the work.
rulings.conditions: Label the CC-BY-licensed material distinctly; give attribution per CC BY 4.0 §3(a).

rulings.quote: Creative Commons has declared the GNU GPL version 3 to be compatible with CC BY-SA 4.0 ... one-way compatibility: content under CC BY-SA 4.0 may be relicensed to GPLv3, but not the other way around.
rulings.rationale: Creative Commons formally declared GPLv3 a compatible license for BY-SA 4.0 in 2015; the direction is BY-SA → GPLv3 only.
rulings.conditions: Only version 4.0; the adapted work must be licensed GPLv3 (not GPLv2).

rulings.quote: The Open Font License (including its original release, version 1.0) is a free copyleft license for fonts. Its only unusual requirement is that when the font is distributed with any program, the program too must be free.
rulings.rationale: Fonts under OFL may ship with software; the font itself stays OFL and cannot be sold on its own.
rulings.conditions: Keep the font under OFL; do not sell the font by itself; Reserved Font Names apply to modified fonts.

rulings.quote: You're under no obligation to choose a license. However, without a license, the default copyright laws apply, meaning that you retain all rights to your source code and no one may reproduce, distribute, or create derivative works from your work.
rulings.rationale: A package with no license (or npm's 'UNLICENSED') grants nothing; you cannot redistribute it under MIT or anything else.
rulings.conditions: Ask the author to add a license, or replace the package.

rulings.quote: Without a license, the default copyright laws apply, meaning that you retain all rights to your source code and no one may reproduce, distribute, or create derivative works from your work.
rulings.rationale: Both sides show 'no declared license' on npm, which is not automatically a problem: it is normal for your own private workspace packages (marked `private: true`, `"license": "UNLICENSED"`) and for commercially-licensed packages that declare `SEE LICENSE IN <file>` (npm maps that to the same LicenseRef marker). Check which case applies before flagging it.
rulings.conditions: Fine if it is your own private/workspace package. If it is a third party's package, you need either a real open-source license or a separate commercial/'SEE LICENSE IN' grant you can point to — an npm dependency with truly no license and no such grant may not be redistributed.

rulings.quote: This is a free software license; it has a copyleft that is not strong, but incompatible with the GNU GPL. We urge you not to use the Ms-PL for this reason.
rulings.rationale: Ms-PL requires redistribution under Ms-PL only, which the GPL cannot satisfy.

rulings.quote: This license is compatible with GPLv2 and GPLv3 ... The EUPL allows relicensing to GPLv2 only and GPLv3 only, because those licenses are listed as two of the alternative licenses
rulings.rationale: EUPL 1.2's Appendix lists GPL v2 and v3 as compatible licenses for derivative works.
rulings.conditions: Use the EUPL compatibility clause (Article 5); the combined work goes out under GPLv3.

rulings.quote: The EUPL allows relicensing to GPLv2 only and GPLv3 only, because those licenses are listed as two of the alternative licenses
rulings.rationale: EUPL's compatibility clause (Appendix, Article 5) is an outbound relicensing option to specific copyleft licenses; it does not permit folding EUPL code into a permissive/MIT project. Treating EUPL like an ordinary permissive dependency would be wrong.
rulings.conditions: Distribute under EUPL-1.2, or use one of the Appendix's listed compatible licenses (GPL-2.0-or-later, GPL-3.0-only, AGPL-3.0-only, LGPL, MPL-2.0, EPL-1.0, CeCILL v2.0, OSL 2.1/3.0) instead of MIT.

rulings.quote: This is a free software license. Its terms are incompatible with the GNU GPL
rulings.rationale: OSL 3.0 has an 'external deployment' copyleft plus terms the GPL does not allow.

rulings.quote: The license of OpenSSL (versions prior to 3.0) is a conjunction of two licenses, one being the license of SSLeay. You must follow both. The combination results in a copyleft free software license that is incompatible with the GNU GPL.
rulings.rationale: The old OpenSSL license has an advertising clause. OpenSSL 3.0+ switched to Apache-2.0, which is fine for GPLv3.
rulings.conditions: Check the OpenSSL version: 3.0 and later are Apache-2.0.

rulings.quote: This license is used by most of PHP4. It is a non-copyleft free software license. It is incompatible with the GNU GPL because it includes strong restrictions on the use of 'PHP' in the name of derived products.
rulings.rationale: Naming restrictions are an added requirement the GPL disallows.

rulings.quote: The NASA Open Source Agreement, version 1.3, is not a free software license because it includes a provision requiring changes to be your 'original creation'.
rulings.rationale: The FSF calls NOSA 1.3 nonfree; the OSI lists it as approved. Either way it is not GPL-compatible.

rulings.rationale: Apache-2.0 code can live inside an MIT project: the Apache files keep their license and NOTICE obligations; your MIT files are unaffected.

rulings.rationale: The MPL's Secondary License mechanism runs outbound (MPL code may additionally go out under GPL); it does not let GPL-3.0-only code come in and let the project stay MPL-only. A project that pulls in GPL-3.0-only code must itself become GPL-3.0.

rulings.quote: May I combine MPL-licensed code and BSD-licensed code in the same executable program? What about Apache? Yes to both.
rulings.rationale: The Mozilla FAQ names Apache explicitly: combining Apache-licensed code with MPL code in the same executable is fine.
rulings.conditions: Keep the Apache NOTICE; only files containing MPL code stay MPL.

rulings.quote: Yes to both. Mozilla currently does this with BSD-licensed code.
rulings.rationale: ISC is the same permissive shape as the BSD license the FAQ names explicitly.
rulings.conditions: Keep the ISC notice.

rulings.quote: May I combine MPL-licensed code and BSD-licensed code in the same executable program? Yes to both. Mozilla currently does this with BSD-licensed code.
rulings.rationale: The Mozilla FAQ names BSD explicitly and says Mozilla itself does this.
rulings.conditions: Keep the BSD notice and no-endorsement clause.

rulings.quote: If you statically link against an LGPLed library, you must also provide your application in an object (not necessarily source) format, so that a user has the opportunity to modify the library and relink the application.
rulings.rationale: MPL-2.0 is a non-copyleft-for-the-project-as-a-whole license (file-level only), so an LGPL library can be linked into it under the ordinary LGPL linking terms — same rule as linking LGPL into MIT.
rulings.conditions: Dynamic linking or relinkable object code; ship LGPL text and library source; permit relinking.

rulings.quote: A permissive license whose main conditions require providing notice of the license.
rulings.rationale: Blue Oak is a modern, notice-only permissive license (patent grant included). The FSF license list does not mention it; OSI approved it 2024-01-19 and the ASF lists it Category A. `jackspeak`, `path-scurry`, `@isaacs/cliui` and `package-json-from-dist` (pulled in by glob 9+ / rimraf / eslint) declare it.
rulings.conditions: Give recipients the license text or a link to it (https://blueoakcouncil.org/license/1.0.0).

rulings.quote: Licensed works, modifications, and larger works may be distributed under different terms and without source code.
rulings.rationale: Permissive; explicitly allows proprietary redistribution.
rulings.conditions: Give recipients the license text or a link to it.

rulings.quote: A permissive license whose main conditions require providing notice of the license. Contributors provide an express grant of patent rights.
rulings.rationale: Notice-only permissive terms with no restriction beyond keeping the license text — the same shape the FSF calls GPL-compatible for MIT/BSD/ISC. The FSF license list has no Blue Oak entry to cite directly, so this ruling relies on the Blue Oak Council's own description plus OSI approval and ASF Category A, not an FSF statement.
rulings.conditions: Give recipients the license text or a link to it.

rulings.quote: The Licensor hereby grants you the right to copy, modify, create derivative works, redistribute, and make non-production use of the Licensed Work.
rulings.rationale: BUSL-1.1 expressly permits copying, modifying and non-production use; production use depends entirely on the package's own Additional Use Grant, and on the Change Date the license converts to its stated Change License (commonly Apache-2.0 or GPL-2.0-or-later). It is source-available, not open source — check the specific package's Additional Use Grant before shipping.
rulings.conditions: Read the package's Additional Use Grant for whether your production use is covered; if not, wait for the Change Date or obtain a commercial license.

rulings.quote: The Licensor's obligations under this Section 13 shall also apply to any of your changes to the Program, and to any changes you make to the Program under Section 4 that alter its behavior.
rulings.rationale: SSPL section 13 requires anyone who offers the software as a service to release the entire 'Service Source Code' (management software, user interfaces, APIs, and everything else needed to run an equivalent service) under SSPL — an obligation GPL-3.0 section 10 does not permit an additional restriction to impose. The OSI Board separately concluded the SSPL is not an open source license.
rulings.conditions: Keep the SSPL component as a separately distributed module; do not offer the combined GPLv3 work as a hosted service.

dissent.claim: The SSPL is Not an Open Source License.

rulings.quote: If you make the functionality of the Program or a modified version available to third parties as a service, you must make the Service Source Code available.
rulings.rationale: SSPL only imposes its whole-stack copyleft on someone who offers the software AS A SERVICE. Using an SSPL-licensed database or tool internally, or shipping it unmodified, does not by itself trigger section 13.
rulings.conditions: Do not offer the SSPL software (or a modified version) as a hosted service to third parties without releasing the Service Source Code under SSPL; internal/unmodified use carries no disclosure obligation.

rulings.quote: The Licensor's obligations under this Section 13 shall also apply to any of your changes to the Program.
rulings.rationale: Offering SSPL software as a service triggers a copyleft over your whole service stack; an MIT project cannot carry that obligation and remain MIT.
rulings.conditions: Only if you never offer the software as a service (see the 'separate' ruling), and even then your distribution cannot be MIT for the SSPL parts themselves.
